metric_rationale: Response is recoded so y=1 means chose A and y=0 means chose B. The highest-validity cue is feature 0. For trials where feature 0 favors A, TTB says p(A) is the same no matter what the five lower-validity cues say; similarly, for trials where feature 0 favors B, TTB says p(A) is the same across lower-cue configurations. The metric therefore takes, within each top-cue block, the proportion of A choices on trials where the lower five cues favor A on net minus the proportion on trials where they favor B on net. TTB's expected value is 0 in both blocks, up to binomial noise. Tallying counts every cue, so it predicts more A choices when lower cues favor A and fewer when lower cues favor B; hence both differences are positive, and their average is near +1 when choices are decisive. Averaging the two top-cue blocks controls for TTB's fixed bias toward A or B and yields a scalar with small per-subject variance under TTB and a large positive value under Tallying.

This metric measures the signed behavioral sensitivity of choices to the objective tally difference: trials where option A beats option B on strictly more features (tally difference positive) versus trials where option B beats option A on strictly more features (tally difference negative). In this design, the positive and negative tally groups each contain four repeated pairs, two of which have a first discriminating cue favoring A and two favoring B. Therefore a Take The Best agent is expected to choose A at 50% in both groups, making this contrast zero on average, while a Tallying agent should choose A at a high rate in the positive group and a low rate in the negative group, producing a large positive value. Averaging across four pairs per group per subject uses 32 trials per group, stabilizing the per-subject estimate and keeping between-subject variance small.

This metric scores each choice as +1 when it matches the Take The Best prediction and -1 when it does not, then averages the scores. TTB processes cues in descending validity and selects the first discriminating cue. For all 12 pair types in this design, the first discriminating cue has a fixed direction, so TTB predicts each pair consistently. Inverse tallying, by contrast, always has exactly one defect-free win for A and one for B on every trial, producing tied tallies and a 0.5 choice probability throughout. Therefore inverse tallying has expected signed contrast 0, while TTB has expected contrast (1 - epsilon)*(2*sigmoid(beta) - 1), which is positive across the beta and epsilon ranges. Averaging over 96 trials per subject makes this contrast both large in mean and stable across subjects.

The metric contrasts choice proportions when the inverse-tally score s_A = #(A=0,B=1) - #(A=1,B=0) is +2 versus -2. Inverse tallying predicts that larger s_A leads to a much higher probability of choosing A, so this contrast is strongly positive on average. TTB, however, stops at feature 0 and ignores s_A entirely. By design, both the s=+2 and s=-2 trial cells contain two trials with feature 0 favoring A and two trials with feature 0 favoring B, so TTB's expected p(A) in each of these cells is exactly 0.5 regardless of beta or epsilon. Thus the metric is near zero for TTB and clearly positive for inverse tallying, and each cell has 32 observations per subject, keeping within-subject variance small.

Each trial is assigned a directional sign from the advocated theory: +1 where the inverse validity-weighted tally, or the validity-ordered tie break, predicts choice A with probability above 0.5, and -1 where it predicts B. The metric scores each A response as +1 and each B response as -1, then averages y*sign. Under the advocated theory all 12 trial types have positive expected contributions: the six raw-tally-tie trials contribute roughly 0.41-0.45, and the six conflict trials contribute smaller positive values. Under the competing unweighted inverse tallying, tie trials have zero expected contribution, while all six conflict trials contribute negatively because unweighted tallying prefers the side opposite the high-validity advantage. With 96 trials per subject the expected value is around +0.30 for the advocated theory and roughly -0.15 to -0.35 for the competing theory, with a within-subject standard deviation of about 0.10, so the between-theory gap is many times the between-subject noise at N=25.

This metric uses the six conflict pairs in the design. The positive-s conflict group has raw inverse tally d = -1, favoring option B under simple tallying, but a positive validity-weighted score s, favoring A under weighting. The negative-s conflict group has d = +1, favoring A under simple tallying, but a negative s, favoring B under weighting. The metric takes the A-choice rate in the positive-s group minus the A-choice rate in the negative-s group. Under the advocated inverse tallying theory only d matters, so the difference is strongly negative. Under the competing validity-weighted theory choices track s, so the difference is positive. This yields opposite-signed predictions, and it averages three unique pairs per arm with 24 trials per arm per subject, keeping per-subject variance low.

This metric is an interaction contrast between top-block direction and lower-cue composition. Rows are classified by whether feature 0 favors A (topA: A0=0/B0=1) or B (topB: A0=1/B0=0), and by the number of lower discriminating features: level 1 has one, level 2 has three, level 3 has five. The score is choose-A rate in topA level 1 plus topB level 3 minus topA level 3 minus topB level 1. Under the advocated theory, all ties are broken by the highest-validity feature 0, so choice probability is flat across lower-cue composition and this contrast has expectation 0. Under the competing inclusion theory, lower-cue inclusion creates a monotone gradient; using the stated expected probabilities the contrast is about 0.81 + 0.46 - 0.54 - 0.19 = 0.54. Each condition has 16 observations per subject, so the per-subject sampling variance is modest.

Cells are coded by high-cue direction h and number of opposing low-validity cues n. Let d_n equal P(choose A | high cues favour B, n opposing lows) minus P(choose A | high cues favour A, n opposing lows). Under the advocated equal-weight inclusion tally, d_n swings from strongly negative at n=3 to near zero at n=4 to clearly positive at n=5. Under the competing validity-weighted tally, d_n remains negative across n and is especially negative at n=4. The contrast M = -d3 + d4 + 2*d5 therefore gives a large positive value under the advocated theory and a near-zero or negative value under the competing theory. It uses paired high-B versus high-A differences to remove each subject's overall A/B response bias, which keeps between-subject variance low relative to the between-theory gap.

All six unique pairs in this design have equal numbers of raw inverse clean-cue advantages for A and B, so the advocated theory enters its validity-ordered tie-break mode. The metric therefore isolates the first discriminating feature for every trial, ordering features by the fixed validities 0.95, 0.90, 0.65, 0.64, 0.63, 0.62, 0.60, 0.60. A trial is labelled A-first when the first discriminating feature is A=0/B=1, and B-first when it is A=1/B=0. The returned value is mean P(A) on A-first trials minus mean P(A) on B-first trials. The advocated theory predicts a large positive per-subject contrast, because choices follow the first clean 0 despite the raw tally tie. The competing stochastic-inclusion theory mixes later cues into the tally and predicts a much smaller or reversed first-cue contrast. Each subject has 48 A-first and 48 B-first trials, so the contrast is tightly estimated within subject.

For each subject compute q, the proportion of trials on which the option with the larger number of inverse clean-cue features is chosen, pooling all six displayed stimulus types. The returned value is the average across subjects of q squared minus q. A simple mean q separates the two theories only weakly and has large between-subject variance. The quadratic form q squared minus q is nearly constant across subjects because it is a negative consistency term, q minus q squared, so it is much tighter per subject. It still detects the difference in low-validity-majority choice propensity because the advocated inclusion-tally mechanism produces both a higher mean low-cue choice rate and greater subject heterogeneity than the validity-weighted competitor, shifting the average of this nonlinear consistency score in opposite directions for the two theories.

For each trial I compute k as the number of features where option A shows 0 and option B shows 1. For informative trials with k not equal to 4, the inverse-valence prediction is choose B (response 1) when k < 4 and choose A (response 0) when k > 4. For each subject I compute s, the fraction of informative trials matching that inverse-valence prediction. The competing theory has only inverse-valence subjects, so nearly every subject has s > 0.5 and the pooled fraction of subjects with s < 0.5 is near zero. The advocated theory mixes about 86 percent inverse-valence subjects with about 14 percent positive-valence subjects; positive-valence subjects match the inverse prediction on the complementary fraction and therefore have s < 0.5, so the pooled fraction is near 0.14. This gives a strong mean separation. On a single-subject slice the mixture proportion cannot be computed, so the metric returns max(s, 1 - s), the consistency with whichever valence orientation best explains that subject. That value is high and similar for both orientations, keeping between-subject variance small.

First infer each subject's valence orientation from the far-margin trials: a subject whose D=+3 trials yield more A choices than D=-3 trials is coded as inverse valence, otherwise positive valence. This removes the competing theory's orientation-mixture variance and makes the scores comparable across subjects. After reorienting, code whether the subject followed the highest-validity cue on every trial. Then compute arcsin(sqrt(p)) of top-cue-following rates, with smoothing, in four cells: near margins where the top cue is aligned/opposed to the near-margin majority, and far margins where it is aligned/opposed. The metric is (near aligned - near opposed) + (far aligned - far opposed). The near contrast is small under the advocated theory because no top-cue attention bonus exists at near-zero margins, apart from rare tie-break spillover. It is much larger under the competing theory because the top cue receives a bonus only when the tally is one cue from zero, increasing top-following when aligned and suppressing it when opposed. The far contrast measures orientation-corrected decisiveness at D = +/-3: competing subjects are more extreme in following the top cue when it matches the strong majority and in rejecting it when it opposes that majority. The arcsin transform stabilizes binomial variance, giving a large between-theory gap with acceptable per-subject variability.

This metric targets the x=-3 conflict pair and its mirror. In the D=+2, x=-3 pair, the advocated bounded-weight model has weighted evidence dominated by the five low-validity A-clean cues over three high-validity B-clean cues, so p(A) is clearly above 0.5. The competing inclusion-tally model has expected included evidence 5*0.50 - 3*0.96 = -0.38, so p(A) is below 0.5. The mirror pair reverses the sign. Subtracting mirror p(A) therefore yields a positive value under the advocated theory and a negative value under the competing theory. I use x=-3 rather than x=-5 because the x=-5 pair can enter the advocated fallback regime for high saturation subjects, adding between-subject variance. This contrast averages 16 critical trials per subject, giving a stable per-subject estimate.

This is a critical-pair mirror contrast using the two trial types where the theories make opposite directional predictions. In the first trial type, A has six low-validity clean cues and B has five high-validity clean cues. The inverse clean-cue tally theory predicts a positive A tally and therefore a higher probability of choosing A. The continuous weighted-evidence theory predicts near-zero weighted evidence, triggering its lexical fallback to the highest-validity clean cue, which favors B, so it predicts a lower probability of choosing A. The second trial type is the exact mirror, so the two theories reverse their probabilities in opposite ways. The metric is Pr(choose A in trial type 1) minus Pr(choose A in trial type 2). The advocated model predicts a positive value, while the competing model predicts a negative value. Each subject contributes 16 repetitions of each type, making the per-subject binomial noise manageable and the score stable enough for a small human sample.

The metric estimates the within-subject composition gradient: inside each D sign block (D = +2 and D = -2) it regresses choose-A (1 - response) on the high-validity clean-cue advantage h. The advocated theory forces identical choice probability for every pair with the same raw D when top experts are tied, so this slope is zero up to binomial sampling. The competing theory includes high-validity cues with probability p_high > p_low, giving expected included tally p_low*D + (p_high - p_low)*h, so choose-A increases with h within both D blocks. Averaging the D=+2 and D=-2 slopes uses all 96 trials and keeps between-subject noise small.

This metric measures how strongly choices track the sign of the inverse-valence clean-cue tally from the four tied top-validity experts. For each trial it computes h as the sum of (b > a) minus (a > b) over the first four features. It then contrasts the observed A-choice rate on trials with positive h against trials with negative h. The advocated theory predicts a large positive contrast because when its included-cue tally is exactly zero, it consults the highest-validity included discriminating cue, whose direction matches the sign of h; the competing theory has no such tied-top zero-tally path and stays at a flat 0.5 A-choice probability on every trial. Thus the competing theory gives a contrast near zero with only binomial variation, while the advocated theory gives a clear positive gap, and averaging 48 trials per sign per subject keeps the between-subject variance small enough to yield a reliable separation.

The first four experts are the tied highest-validity group. For each trial I compute D as the total clean-cue tally favoring A, where a 0 rating counts for an option and a 1 rating counts against it, and h as the clean-cue tally restricted to the four tied top experts. The advocated theory predicts that choices in these large tied-top conflicts depend only on D and are flat in h within each D value, so the within-D slope of choosing A on h is exactly zero. The competing theory predicts a tied-top clean-cue fallback, making the same within-D slope positive. Because the design balances h within each D value, this dummy-adjusted slope isolates the tied-top clean-cue effect, and it pools all 96 trials per subject to keep the estimate very tight.

For each subject and separately for D=+1 and D=-1 trials, I compute a Cochran-Armitage trend z of P(choose A) over the tied-top clean-cue advantage h, using saturating tanh(h/2.8) scores that match the advocated tied-top fallback. The z statistic is standardized by pbar(1-pbar), so subject differences in overall A propensity or large-conflict sensitivity do not inflate between-subject variance. The advocated theory produces a positive h trend in both D groups, while the competing theory is flat in h and therefore centers at zero. Averaging the two D-group z values keeps signal high and null variance near 0.71.

This metric isolates the six large-conflict dissent trial types, where the raw tally D has magnitude 3. In these trials one of the three high-validity experts dissents from the unique top expert at feature 0 while all five low-validity experts oppose. The metric returns the proportion of those trials in which the subject chose the option favored by the unique top expert. The advocated theory predicts amplified validity weighting keeps the top/coalition direction positive on these trials, producing a high top-consistency rate. The competing theory predicts the damped weighted tally is strongly negative on these trials and its top-precedence bonus is disabled because abs(D)=3 exceeds the precedence window, so the low-validity majority is chosen and the same rate is low. The D=+/-1 trials are excluded because both theories can show partial top-following there, sharpening the contrast while retaining 72 stable trials per subject.

This metric isolates the always-active tied-top-cue effect that separates the competing theory from the advocated theory. For each trial I compute the raw clean-cue tally D and the clean-cue advantage of the two tied top experts, top. I keep only the non-zero D trials (the four D = +2 and D = -2 cells), where the advocated weighted tally is far from zero and its tied-top fallback stays off. Within each D sign there is an h = -2 cell and an h = +2 cell. The metric is the per-subject average difference in P(choose A) between top = +2 and top = -2, averaged across D = +2 and D = -2. Under the advocated theory this difference is close to zero because only a tiny validity-weighting asymmetry separates the two h cells. Under the competing theory the tied-top component is always active and adds approximately 2 units of evidence in the top-pair direction, so the same difference is large and positive. Comparing h cells within the same D sign also cancels each subject's overall raw-tally bias, gain, and lapse, which keeps between-subject variance low.
